newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian poll candidate urges clear line on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian poll candidate urges clear line on NATO.

text.p: The main opposition candidate in Bulgaria's presidential election this month has called for his country to make a concerted effort to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

"Bulgaria should give a clear answer to the question of how to establish foreign guarantees for its national security," Petar Stoyanov, who is tipped by public opinion polls as the front-runner for the October 27 vote, said during the first televised debate of the campaign on Thursday night.
"Bulgaria could be a member of an international organisation which is able to guarantee its interests, and I can name this organisation right now -- the North Atlantic Treaty," he added.
Stoyanov said during the debate that other former Warsaw Pact states had made their desire to join NATO clear and Bulgaria should do the same.
The Balkan country's anti-leftist opposition is keen to bring the Balkan country into NATO while the ruling Socialists want to avoid upsetting Russia.
"We think the the question should not be put in terms of "for' and "against' but "when' and "how', because Bulgaria should decide for itself the right moment to join NATO," Stoyanov said.

Irina Bokov, vice-presidential running mate of the ruling party candidate Ivan Marazov, said the question should be decided by parliament, in which the Socialists have a majority, and by the Bulgarian people, not simply the government.
NATO is likely to decide some time next year which former communist states to draw into its movement eastward and Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and possibly Slovenia are seen as the favourites.
Other East European countries such as Romania and Slovakia which are not seen as front-runners have launched campaigns to persuade the alliance to let them in the first expansion wave.
The latest survey from polling agency MBMD puts Stoyanov in the lead with 31 percent support, followed by Marazov with 20 percent.

Television viewers commented that Stoyanov spoke clearly and without notes, making frequent references to the future, while Marazov, who is culture minister in the present government, referred often to Bulgaria's recent past.
The Central Electoral Committee has registered 13 candidacies for the election. If no one wins an outright majority, a second round will be held a week later.
President Zhelyu Zhelev, who came to power after former Communist ruler Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, lost a U.S.-style party primary and is not contesting the poll.
